description: Release-pace scoreboard: new features named in release notes inside the window. Generated by scripts/compute-pace.mjs from data/releases/; do not edit by hand.
rules: Counts new features named in release notes dated inside the window.
Fixes, speed-ups and reliability items are not counted, for any app.
A release whose notes repeat the previous release word for word adds nothing.
Boilerplate such as "Bug fixes and improvements" names nothing and adds nothing.
Where a note is ambiguous between new and improved, a competitor’s item is counted as new.
Releases not yet classified by a person are listed under pendingReview and add nothing.
notCounted tallies are for transparency only and are not comparable between apps: fix lines in App Store notes were not itemized exhaustively.

apps.name: SPLYT

counted.feature: Plan a workout straight from the + on your home screen, instead of going out to the workout picker.
Read a friend’s workout history — tap the name at the top of History to switch whose sessions you are looking at, the same way you switch whose recap you read on Stats.
Your day’s activity is grouped by what kind of thing it was — Strength, Cardio, Sports and Recovery — each with its own total, and the whole day’s total beside the Activity heading.
Did the same thing more than once? It folds into a single row you can tap open to see each session. Workouts stay listed on their own, since each already has its own name.

Your weekly and monthly recaps break the week down by what you actually did — how many lifts, and how long you spent on cardio, sport and recovery. A kind you did not do that week simply is not listed.
Share your whole day, not just one workout. Open your ring from the home screen and Share Day builds the same cards a finished workout gets, for everything you did.
Share a single activity out of a grouped session — the sauna on its own, not the lift it followed.
Move a whole planned session to another day in one go. Every activity in it keeps its own time.
Pick how your home Activity section reads. Settings → Home View → Activity Layout: grouped by type with a total per kind, or one list in the order things happened. Grouped stays the default.
Editing a planned activity now opens the same builder you use to make a template — pick movements, set reps and weights, superset and reorder — and you can change the day and time without leaving it.

Share the shape of your run. An outdoor run, ride or walk now leads its share gallery with a Route card — distance, pace and time over the trace of where you went, on a clear background so you can drop it straight onto your own photo of the place. Pick the line’s colour; it starts on your accent.

Call off a planned session from the editor you opened it in. Remove one activity from a day that holds several, or take the whole session off the day — and for a repeating plan, choose whether it’s just this day or every one from here on.

Bring your training history over from Strong or Hevy. Export from the other app and share it straight into Splyt, or pick the file yourself from Profile → Import Data. Splyt shows you what it found — how many workouts, over what dates, which movements are new to you — before anything is added, and every session lands on the day you actually trained.
Imported workouts count. They sit on their real dates in your training calendar and feed your stats, records and totals like anything you logged here yourself.

Changed your mind? Profile → Import Data → Last import lists everything you’ve brought in, from which app, with every workout it added — and undoes any one of them on its own. Undoing what came from Strong leaves what came from Hevy exactly where it is.

Your weekly and monthly recaps now show the training calendar itself — the week laid out the way it reads everywhere else in the app, instead of a separate summary that had to be matched up in your head.
Previewing a workout someone shared with you shows the workout, not a summary of it.

Step competitions you can watch. A race against your friends now runs in a world — a road, a gym, a pool — with a character you pick and can change. Your steps move you along it, and the map replays what happened while you were away.
A run, ride or swim competition is won on distance, not on how many sessions you logged. Three short jogs no longer beat one long run.
Two people get a head-to-head instead of a leaderboard, and a finished race opens on its result and tells you when it ended.
Invite links show the race itself — who is asking, what the competition is, and when it actually runs — instead of a bare link.
A competition widget and a multi-habit widget for your home screen.
You can attach screenshots to feedback, so a bug you can see is a bug you can show.
A brand-new account is offered the founders as a first friend, instead of an empty Friends tab.

A group competition invite now waits for your answer. Accept and Decline actually do something — until you accept you are not on the start line, and the standings list who was invited and has not replied yet instead of showing them at zero, which read as losing badly rather than as not playing.

The competition map shows who is training right now. On a lifting competition it also shows what they have put up so far in the session — kept separate from the leaderboard, which still only counts workouts you have finished.
You can add a friend to a competition without sending them a link. If they are already on Splyt, put them straight in.
Hold a message in a competition chat to report it or block the person who sent it.

A competition that hasn’t started yet opens on its own fight card — everyone who is in it, stood up together with the date underneath, instead of an empty race with the whole field sat on zero. Works for a group and for a one-on-one, where it bills the matchup.
Accept or decline a competition invite straight from the notification, on your phone or your watch, without opening the app.
You can leave a group competition you joined. Your score comes off the board and the race carries on without you.

When somebody leaves a competition you are in, you are told — and if they were the last one racing you, the standings say so and offer to bring somebody else in or close it out. Anyone who has left is now listed under the board, so a race that gets quieter explains itself.
You can leave a one-on-one competition too. Because a versus cannot carry on with one person, leaving retires it for both of you and lets the other person know.

Planning a split now starts by picking its shape. Six common weeks — full body, upper/lower, push/pull/legs and more — each drawn day by day with the muscles it trains, so you can choose by looking. Pick one and the week fills in with named days you can then build however you like, or start from a blank week as before.

Tapping a notification about a friend’s gym trip now opens the whole trip as one session — the lift, the sauna and the jacuzzi together, with the totals for all of it — instead of whichever single part the link pointed at.
Hold a message in a competition chat to report it or block whoever sent it.

Any saved workout can now be sent as a link. Whoever opens it sees the whole workout — every set, the weights and reps, your warm-up and top sets, supersets round by round, drop sets and rests, and any note you left on a movement — in a page that works without Splyt and without an account. Share a workout from your Saved tab and the link is what gets sent.
If they already have Splyt, the link opens straight into the app on the workout, ready to save to their own library.
Pick a light or dark style for a workout recap before you post it.

The founders can now start a conversation with you. Until now that chat only worked one way — you had to write first. If we message you it arrives like any other notification, and tapping it opens the chat so you can just reply.

Your Apple Watch counts reps on lat pulldowns and straight-arm pulldowns. Pull-ups and chin-ups are deliberately left out — there your hands stay fixed to the bar and your body moves past them, so there is nothing at the wrist to count.

A setting for whether your phone alerts you when a rest period ends while you are wearing your watch. On by default — a wrist buzz is easy to miss under a working set, and a watch cannot put a sound in the headphones you already have on.

See a friend’s training week from your own calendar. Tap the avatar in the Training Calendar header and pick anyone you are friends with — their planned and completed days, read-only. It used to mean leaving your calendar, finding their profile and opening theirs.
The competition widget is free for everyone. Put your race on your home screen whether or not you are on Pro.
Get a notification when somebody joins a group competition you are in, so the standings never quietly grow a name you do not recognise.
Swap one activity of a planned day without rebuilding the whole day.
Splits have a home of their own. Open the training calendar and tap the grid to pick a proven split, sorted by how many days a week you can train, or build one by hand.
Splits can roll instead of repeating on weekdays. Four days on, one off keeps going round whatever day it lands on, so your week no longer has to be seven days long.
Generating a split now asks properly: which days work best, what you want to bring up, and what hurts and how. Injuries get the movement swapped rather than the day skipped.
Review what a split puts on your calendar before it puts it there.
When you pick a time to train, Splyt now tells you the hour you usually train — and says something if that time collides with your sleep.

Create your own character. Describe anything — a purple bear, a lightbulb, your dog — or use a photo, see it drawn in about a minute, and a few minutes later it is yours on the road: running, swimming, lifting, cheering on the podium. Pro includes one a month.

The character library. Everything anyone has made and shared, free for everyone to use. Search it, or just browse; if someone already made what you were about to describe, Splyt offers it before you build your own.
Your workout picker, rebuilt around what you actually pick: your recent workouts first, search at the top, and one tap to start anything.

Reorder a split by dragging. Hold a session to move it within its day, or hold a day’s number to move the whole day — everything in it comes along. Planned Monday’s workouts and want them on Tuesday? Drag the day.
Your character has its own place in Settings now, with the one you race as right there in the row. It was buried at the bottom of Appearance.
Make me. A selfie for your face, a head-to-toe photo for your build, and the outfit you want — the clothes you’re wearing or ones you describe. Animated or fully realistic. Private to you, always.
Creating a character is one thing at a time now: describe it, start from a photo, or make yourself. No more guessing whether to type and upload.
Famous faces. Describe a real person and they come out as themselves — in what they are known for, at their real height. A 7'4" centre towers over the field.
When a competition ends: how far your steps would have taken you, on a real map, with everyone on the line — and every person gets an award that is true of their week.
Race chat: a message from the group buzzes your phone, and tapping it opens the chat. Tap a photo to see it full screen, pinch to zoom, save or share it. And you can take a photo, not just pick one.
Import a whole plan at once: pick every screenshot your trainer sent in one go and they come in as one split, in order.
Swipe a saved split to delete it.
A step competition now reads your watch too, and nudges anyone whose count has gone quiet.

The live workout, redesigned. The sheet is a card tucked under the status bar; your workout’s name and the clock sit at the top with Finish and a menu beside them; every movement is its own card on a darker list, with a set’s weight and reps as “45 lbs × 6 reps” and a finished set washed in your colour. The bottom drawer is gone: a floating pill holds the mic and add, and while you rest it says how long is left — drag it sideways to change the rest, tap it for fifteen more seconds.

Say your split. Tap the mic in the split builder and describe your week — “push, pull, legs, rest, repeat, everything at 3 PM, stairs after” — and it lands as your week, days and times in place. It hears how long to run it (“for six weeks”, “until the end of October”) and when to start (“from Monday”), and weeks that differ.
Press and hold a planned workout in the training calendar and carry it to another day.
A rest day can still carry a session — a swim on your rest day — and it is still a rest day.
Tapping a movement in a workout summary opens the exercise.
Mid-workout, the This Week bars answer back: press a day to read it, tap one to see the sessions behind it — what each was called, when it started, how long, how much.
Made a competition? You can now take someone out of it — Remove someone, under the cog on the race. Their score comes off the board and the race carries on.
The training calendar walks you through it the first time: where your splits live, and the plus that plans a day.
Mid-workout, searching the exercise list for an activity — a walk, basketball — offers the activity list instead of nothing.
Share a split straight from the split itself. Pick a friend and it lands under their From friends.
With one saved workout or none, the workout picker offers Build a workout and Plan your week right there.
The home calendar hint shows a real week the way the training calendar draws one, and offers Create a split?

The Vessel. Swipe right from any live activity and watch a glass fill as you go, past the marks for last time, your typical and your best, with your heart rate and calories against a typical session and this week’s bars growing under it. Lifts race the weight you have moved, not the clock: a template against its own previous runs, a labelled day against days with the same label. Flip it to Graph for your heart rate over time with last time’s as a ghost.
A lift pages sideways like every other activity: your sets, then the Vessel, then your rings.
Ask the coach about a movement and it shows the movement’s card, with a tap into your history and how to do it.
The coach remembers the photo you sent. Ask “what’s it called?” a week later and it still knows.
Searching Select a workout for basketball or a sauna offers the activity list, with your search carried over. And once you type, the buttons and folders step aside so the results have the room.

Share a workout with anyone. Share Workout now has Copy Link, and the link rides along when you share a card — it opens your full summary as a web page, laid out exactly like the app: every set, your effort, the map, the records. No Splyt needed to see it.

Your friends’ friends. Open any friend’s profile and their friends are listed at the bottom, each with an Add button — so when one person from your gym gets on Splyt, the rest are a tap away through them.

A new Friends tab for your first day. Before you have anyone on Splyt it now leads with what friends are for, offers the people who built the app as first friends — tap either one to read their story, see their numbers and their latest session before you add them — and puts Invite friends where your thumb is.
Use these sets — paste the sets from a past session straight onto the movement you are working on.
Workout settings open from the menu during a live workout, and what you change applies right away instead of next time.
Press a bar in This Week to open that day’s sessions.
Tapping a friend’s name in your plan’s day opens what they trained.
Signing back in, the app remembers how you did it last time — Apple, Google or email — and marks that button “Last used”, so you land back in your own account instead of starting a new one.
Your Apple Watch opens on a microphone. Tap it, say what you’re doing — “basketball”, “start my plan”, “rest day” — and it counts down 3-2-1 and starts. The full list is one scroll down.
Adding an activity to a workout on the watch works the same way: say “add a basketball session”.
During a rest on the watch, swipe across to control your music.
Your Weekly Recap goes deeper: PRs you set, this week against last, weight, progress photos, steps, sleep, recovery and habits.
Send your week to your trainer: pick what to include, then share a link that opens in any browser, or export a PDF.

Send your week to your trainer. The Weekly Recap now exports a full report — your training day by day, PRs, weight, steps, sleep and habits — as a PDF or a private link that opens in any browser. Choose what goes in it before you send.

Setting up Splyt is a different experience: one welcome screen with Apple or Google sign-in that remembers how you got in last time, your split built with you, and a workout that plays itself so you can see how logging works before you lift anything.
The split planner and Proven splits have been rebuilt — clearer days, clearer weeks, and scheduling that moves forward instead of dropping you back at the picker.
Correct sets you have already logged by voice. “I started with 10 pounds and then did 30 for the rest” now fixes the sets that are there instead of adding new ones underneath them.
A new account gets the Training Calendar widget free for its first week.
A template’s graph page shows your last few times doing it, so you can see the trend rather than one week of it.

Copy a day on your training calendar. An empty day now has a copy button — pick a day you have already planned or trained, take the whole thing or just one activity from it, and it lands with its times.
Splyt opens with a new launch animation — the wordmark splits down the middle and pulls back to your Home.
On the watch, swipe right on the rest timer to see what’s coming: your next set’s weight and reps, which set it is, and its warm-up or drop tag — or the next movement once you’ve finished one.

Ask for your numbers from another movement — "put my leg curl weights on the leg extension" — and Splyt fills them in. You can name a movement however you say it out loud; it matches what you are already doing.
The first time you land on Home, Splyt shows you where your training calendar lives: it pulls the date down for you, holds the week open for a moment, and puts it back.
Your monthly recap now has everything the weekly one has — PRs, weight, progress photos, steps, sleep, recovery and habits — drawn week by week, with this month set against last.

Grips and handles. On movements like the lat pulldown, rows, curls and pushdowns, tap the V beside the name and pick how you’re doing it — wide bar, V-handle, rope, one arm — from pictures. Your “last time” weights now come from the same grip, and you can change the grip for a single set from the keypad.

Load the bar. On a barbell lift, tap the barbell on the keypad and tap the plates you’ve put on — Splyt does the math and fills in the weight. It opens already loaded with whatever you typed, so it tells you what to put on, too.
Set your grip from your watch. On a movement’s sets, tap Grip under the swap button and pick the handle, grip or width — rope, V-handle, wide bar, one arm. It shows on your phone straight away.
Picked a proven split like Push / Pull / Legs? One tap fills every day with starter exercises — sets and reps included — and you see them before anything is saved.

Stats has a new “Against your history” card: your latest session of an activity next to your last, usual and best — the same glass and heart-rate graph as during a workout — with chips to switch between the things you do most. The cramped version on the workout summary is gone.
Try Pro free for a week. Every plan now starts with a 7-day free trial — cancel any time before it ends and you are not charged.

Partials. Finished a set with half reps to failure? Add partials from the set’s menu, or just say it — “the last three sets I did partials to failure after each”. They count toward your volume at half a rep each.

Your history knows the grip. A movement’s history now includes the times you logged it under its old names (“Cable Pushdown (With Rope Attachment)” counts as Cable Pushdown on the rope), and chips at the top filter the chart, records and history to one grip.

Search for a grip — “rope pushdown”, “wide grip pull-up” — and the movement is added with that grip already picked. Saying it to the voice logger works the same way, and templates remember the grip too.

Log in kilograms. Pick it once — in Workout Defaults, or from any movement’s ⋯ menu — and everything follows: your sets, your watch, your body weight, your stats, your recaps and what Splyt AI tells you. Past workouts included. Your training is stored exactly as you logged it; only the number on screen changes.
Outside the US, Splyt now starts you in kilograms instead of pounds. Change it any time and your choice sticks.
Switch an exercise from your watch. On a movement’s sets, swap it for something similar without reaching for your phone — and sets you have already logged stay with the movement that earned them.

Tell the voice logger your whole day, not one workout. “Legs at 3, a run around 4, then a swim in the evening” becomes three separate workouts, each with its own activity, time and distance. Say them in any order, as vaguely as you like.
Searching to start a workout now finds your saved workouts too. Start typing a template’s name and it appears above the activity list, ready to go.
